answer: A molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule (e.g., $C_4H_{10}$ for butane). It does NOT provide information about how the atoms are connected or arranged : i.e., no structural information.

answer: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound (e.g., $CH_2O$ for glucose). A molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms in one molecule (e.g., $C_6H_{12}O_6$ for glucose). The molecular formula is always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.

answer: A condensed structural formula groups atoms around each carbon without drawing individual bonds. Hydrogen atoms are written next to the carbon they are attached to, and side chains or functional groups are shown in brackets. Example: butane is written as $CH_3(CH_2)_2CH_3$.

answer: In a skeletal formula, carbon atoms and the hydrogen atoms bonded to them are not explicitly shown. Each vertex and each end of a line represents a carbon atom. Heteroatoms (O, N, halogens, etc.) and their attached hydrogens are written explicitly.

answer: A solid wedge represents a bond pointing out of the plane of the paper toward the viewer. A dashed wedge (or hash) represents a bond pointing behind the plane of the paper, away from the viewer. A normal thin line represents a bond lying in the plane of the paper.

answer: A dot-and-cross diagram shows the distribution of valence electrons between atoms. Dots represent electrons from one atom and crosses represent electrons from another, illustrating both bonding pairs and lone pairs in a molecule.

answer: A functional group is an atom or group of atoms attached to a carbon chain or ring that determines the characteristic chemical properties of an organic compound. Chemical reactions primarily occur at the functional group. Examples: $-OH$ (hydroxyl) in alcohols, $-COOH$ (carboxyl) in carboxylic acids.
prompt: Define a functional group in organic chemistry.

answer: The functional group of alcohols is the hydroxyl group ($-OH$). The general formula for the alcohol homologous series is $C_nH_{2n+1}OH$. Example: Ethanol ($CH_3CH_2OH$).

answer: Isomerism is the phenomenon where two or more compounds possess the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements or spatial orientations of atoms, resulting in different physical and chemical properties.

answer: Chain isomerism arises from differences in the carbon skeleton (straight vs. branched chain), while positional isomerism arises from different positions of the same functional group on the same carbon skeleton.

answer: Functional group isomerism occurs when compounds have the same molecular formula but contain different functional groups, placing them in different homologous series. Example: Ethanol ($C_2H_5OH$) and dimethyl ether ($CH_3OCH_3$) both have the formula $C_2H_6O$.

answer: Metamerism is a type of structural isomerism where compounds have the same molecular formula and the same functional group but differ in the length of carbon chains on either side of the functional group. It is common in ethers, ketones, and secondary amines.

answer: Tautomerism is a special type of structural isomerism where two isomers (tautomers) exist in dynamic equilibrium due to the migration of a proton ($H^+$) and a double bond between two atoms within the same molecule. The most common example is keto-enol tautomerism, where a ketone (keto form) and an enol form interconvert.
